intro: A week about foundations that hold: the residual stream and its new rivals, entropy, how science changes, and quiet rooms full of light. Pick what you like.
notes: Regenerated mid-week for 2026-W48 after the structure change. No feedback or inbox ideas this week.

items.title: Why residual stacks do not forget their input: a derivation
items.description: Take a stack of L blocks x_{l+1} = x_l + f(x_l). Show that the gradient reaching any layer always keeps a direct identity term. Then show how the variance of the residual stream grows with depth. Last, scale the skip path by a number other than 1 and see what breaks.
items.why: Every transformer is built on this one line. Knowing why it works is what lets you judge new ideas like hyper-connections, this week's New in AI.
steps: Write x_L as x_l plus a sum of block outputs, then differentiate the loss with respect to x_l
Assume each block adds independent zero-mean noise of variance v and find Var(x_L) as a function of L
Replace the skip with lambda times x_l and work out what happens over L layers when lambda is 0.9 or 1.1
Read section 3 of the identity mappings paper and compare with your answer
hints: The sum gives dx_L/dx_l = I + (terms from the blocks).
Independent variances add, so the variance grows linearly in L.
Over L layers the skip path is multiplied by lambda to the power L. Try L = 100.

items.then: Explain in three sentences why lambda must stay close to 1.

items.title: Removal or suppression? Design the test for an unlearned model
items.description: A model says it has forgotten a fact. Design an experiment that tells true removal apart from a model that only hides the answer. Then compare your design with a new paper on this week's list that calibrates unlearning diagnostics with known cases.
items.why: A good control is the heart of a good evaluation. This exercise trains the habit of asking: compared to what?
steps: Write down three ways a model can look like it forgot while the knowledge is still there
For each one, name a measurement that would expose it
Design two anchors where you know the truth: a fact never trained on, and a fact trained on and kept
Read the abstract and setup of the anchors paper and note one thing it does that you missed
hints: Think about refusals, paraphrased questions, and how fast the fact comes back with a little fine-tuning.
A diagnostic is only useful if it gives different readings on the never-trained and the kept anchors.
Suppressed knowledge often returns after a few gradient steps. Absent knowledge does not.

resources.title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
TOFU: A Task of Fictitious Unlearning for LLMs
resources.note: The standard benchmark built on made-up authors, so the truth is known

items.then: Write your test as a one-paragraph protocol someone else could run.

items.title: Hyper-connections: rethinking the residual stream
items.description: The residual connection has barely changed since 2015. Hyper-connections widen it into several parallel streams that the network learns to mix. DeepSeek's mHC made this stable at scale, and this week a new variant on balancing stream mixing was among the most upvoted papers on Hugging Face.
items.why: A trending architecture idea that touches optimisation, stability and efficiency at once. It is a good case study in why a constraint can matter more than extra freedom.

explain.what: Instead of one residual stream, keep n copies. Learnable weights decide how each layer reads from, writes to and mixes the streams.
explain.why: Plain residuals force a fixed trade-off between gradient flow and representation collapse. Learned mixing lets the network choose its own trade-off.
explain.how: Each layer has small matrices that combine the n streams into the layer input and spread the layer output back across the streams.
components: expansion rate n (the number of streams)
depth connections: how layer outputs are written back
width connections: how streams mix with each other
in mHC, a constraint that keeps the mixing matrix doubly stochastic
explain.limitations: Unconstrained mixing can break the identity path and make training unstable at scale. Extra streams also cost memory traffic, which matters more than FLOPs here.
explain.research_relevance: A clear link between architecture and training dynamics. It also shows how a geometric constraint can restore a property that made the original design work.

steps: Do the residual derivation in Research first, so you know what the identity path buys
Read the Hyper-Connections abstract and its main figure, and sketch the n-stream picture yourself
Read Raschka's mHC page and find the one constraint mHC adds and why
Skim the abstract of this week's trending cmHC paper and say what problem it targets
Explain to yourself why a doubly stochastic mixing matrix cannot blow up the signal

items.title: Eigenvectors tell you where a system ends up
items.subject: maths
items.description: Apply a Markov matrix again and again and the state settles down. The place it settles is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. The same idea powers PageRank and the stationary distribution of any random walk.
items.why: Long-run behaviour of repeated linear maps shows up in RNNs, power iteration, PageRank and diffusion. One clear picture covers all of them.
steps: Watch the 3Blue1Brown lesson on eigenvalues and pause to predict each picture
Watch Strang's lecture on Markov matrices and note why 1 is always an eigenvalue
Take a 2 by 2 Markov matrix, multiply a starting vector by it ten times, and watch it converge
Try the Markov question in this week's questions

items.title: What entropy actually counts
items.subject: physics
items.description: Entropy is not disorder. It counts how many microscopic arrangements look the same from outside. The second law is then a statement about probability: systems drift to the macrostates with the most arrangements.
items.why: The same counting sits behind cross-entropy loss, information theory and the cost of erasing a bit. This week's Landauer question builds on it.
steps: Watch the Veritasium video and write down its one-sentence definition of entropy
Read Feynman Vol. I Ch. 44 and find where heat engines lead to entropy
Count arrangements yourself: 4 coins, how many ways to get 2 heads versus 4 heads
Connect S = k ln W to Shannon's H = minus the sum of p log p in your own words

items.title: The Meiji Restoration: how Japan rebuilt itself in one generation
items.subject: history
items.description: In 1868 a small group of samurai overthrew the shogunate and set out to modernise Japan fast. Within about forty years it had railways, a constitution, universal schooling and an industrial economy. How it happened, and at what cost, is one of history's great case studies.
items.why: It explains much of modern Japan and connects with your Japanese practice. It is also a rare natural experiment in deliberate, rapid change.
steps: Watch the Origins video for the big picture
Listen to the Historical Association podcast for the debates historians still have
Read the Meiji chapters of Gordon's book and list three reforms and one thing they cost
Compare with one other country's rapid modernisation you know

items.title: Popper versus Kuhn: how does science really change?
items.subject: philosophy
items.description: Popper said science moves by bold guesses and attempts to refute them. Kuhn said most science is puzzle-solving inside a paradigm, broken by rare revolutions. Both describe something real about how a field like ML behaves.
items.why: This is research taste in its oldest form. It helps you ask whether a result is a refutation, a puzzle solved, or the start of a new paradigm.
steps: Read sections 1 to 3 of the SEP entry on Popper, on falsification
Read the SEP entry on Kuhn, sections on normal science and paradigms
Pick one shift in deep learning, such as the move to transformers, and describe it in Kuhn's terms and then in Popper's
Decide which account fits better and why

cross_domain.connection: Kuhn's normal science looks a lot like benchmark-chasing, and Popper's refutations look like negative results and failure-mode papers.

items.description: Your mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. Lynn Margulis argued this in 1967 against strong doubt, and the evidence slowly won. It is one of the biggest merges in the history of life.
items.why: A great story about an extraordinary claim backed by extraordinary evidence, and about how a field changes its mind.

items.title: Writing was invented more than once
items.subject: linguistics
items.description: Writing appeared independently in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and perhaps Egypt. In Mesopotamia it may have grown out of clay accounting tokens. It began as a data storage technology, not as literature.
items.why: It changes how you see language: speech is ancient and natural, writing is a recent invention. A nice link to how we store and compress information.
steps: Read the Discover article on the separate inventions of writing
Read Schmandt-Besserat's page on how tokens became writing
List what the earliest texts in each place were used for

resources.title: How Humans Invented Writing, Four Different Times
resources.creator: Discover Magazine

resources.title: The Evolution of Writing
resources.creator: Denise Schmandt-Besserat

cross_domain.connection: Early writing was an accounting and storage system. It is a story about inventing a data format before it became a story about language.

items.then: Pair it with Arrival in Culture this week.

items.title: How many boxes until you have all 50 stickers?
items.subject: probability
items.description: Each cereal box has one of 50 stickers, each equally likely. On average, how many boxes do you need to buy to collect all 50?
items.why: Splitting a hard waiting time into easy stages is a trick you will use again and again.
hints: Split the process into stages: you have k different stickers and wait for a new one.
When you have k stickers, a new one comes with probability (50 - k)/50. The wait is geometric.
Add the expected waits and recognise a harmonic sum.
items.solution: The wait in stage k has mean 50/(50 - k). Summing gives 50 times (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/50), which is about 50 times 4.5, so about 225 boxes. In general it is n H_n, roughly n ln n.

items.title: Where does the two-state weather chain settle?
items.subject: maths
items.description: If today is sunny, tomorrow is sunny with probability 0.9. If today is rainy, tomorrow is sunny with probability 0.5. In the long run, what fraction of days are sunny? Find it as an eigenvector.
items.why: A direct practice of this week's maths topic.
hints: Write the transition matrix with rows that sum to 1.
The long-run distribution pi satisfies pi P = pi.
In the long run the flow from sunny to rainy must equal the flow back.
items.solution: Let s be the long-run sunny share. Flow balance gives s times 0.1 = (1 - s) times 0.5, so 0.6 s = 0.5 and s = 5/6. About 83 percent of days are sunny.

items.title: What is the least energy needed to erase one bit?
items.subject: physics
items.description: Landauer's principle says erasing one bit at temperature T must release at least k T ln 2 of heat. Compute this at room temperature, 300 K. Then estimate the minimum for erasing 1 gigabyte.
items.why: It ties this week's entropy topic to computing. Erasure, not computation itself, has a physical floor.
hints: Boltzmann's constant k is about 1.38 times 10 to the minus 23 joules per kelvin.
One gigabyte is about 8 times 10 to the 9 bits.
items.source: R. Landauer, Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process, IBM Journal (1961)
items.solution: k T ln 2 = 1.38e-23 times 300 times 0.693, about 2.9e-21 J per bit. For 8e9 bits that is about 2.3e-11 J, far below what real chips use.

items.title: A skater pulls in her arms. Where does the extra energy come from?
items.subject: physics
items.description: A spinning skater pulls her arms in and halves her moment of inertia. Angular momentum is conserved. By what factor does her spin rate change, and by what factor does her kinetic energy change? Where does the extra energy come from?
items.why: A small puzzle that separates two conserved-looking quantities, only one of which is actually conserved.
hints: L = I times omega stays the same.
Kinetic energy is one half I omega squared. Write it in terms of L and I.
Pulling the arms in takes force over a distance.
items.source: Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 18 (conservation of angular momentum)
items.solution: Halving I doubles omega. Kinetic energy is L squared over 2I, so it doubles. The extra energy is the work her muscles do pulling her arms inward.

items.title: Can hot water freeze faster than cold?
items.description: In 1963 a Tanzanian schoolboy, Erasto Mpemba, noticed that hot ice-cream mix froze faster than cool mix. Physicists argued about it for decades. A 2020 experiment at Simon Fraser University showed a version of the effect in a carefully controlled system, but whether it happens in ordinary freezers is still debated.
items.why: A real scientific mystery that started with a student who refused to drop an odd observation.
steps: Read the Science News piece on the 2020 experiment
Skim the LSBU page for the history and the proposed explanations

items.title: Crossing the Pacific without instruments
items.description: In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti with no compass or charts. Navigator Mau Piailug read the stars, the ocean swells and the flight of birds. The voyage helped show that Polynesians settled the Pacific on purpose, not by drifting.
items.why: A remarkable human skill, and a story about knowledge kept alive by one person and then shared.
steps: Read the Smithsonian Folklife piece
Look at the PBS Wayfinders page on how star compasses work

items.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto: three pieces and a farewell documentary
items.description: Listen to three pieces across his life. Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence (1983): notice how a simple repeating figure carries so much feeling. Energy Flow (1999): a quiet solo piano piece that became a surprise hit in Japan. andata from async (2017): written after his cancer treatment, listen for how sound and silence share the space. Then watch Coda, the 2017 documentary that follows him after his illness and the Fukushima disaster.
items.why: A composer who moved from synth-pop to film scores to ambient work. A rich, calm way into Japanese culture this month.
steps: Listen to the three pieces in order of year, with nothing else on
Watch Coda
Pick the piece that stayed with you and say why in one sentence

items.title: Hammershøi: two quiet rooms to look at slowly
items.description: Vilhelm Hammershøi painted almost empty rooms in his Copenhagen flat. Look at Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams (1900) for five minutes: where does the light come from, and where does it land? Then look at Interior in Strandgade, Sunlight on the Floor (1901) and notice the door, the window shapes on the floor and the stillness.
items.why: Slow looking is a skill. These paintings reward it more than almost any others, and they fit the short winter days.
steps: Open the first painting full screen and look for five minutes without reading anything
Read the museum notes

items.description: Watch Denis Villeneuve's Arrival (2016), where a linguist learns an alien written language. Then read Ted Chiang's novella Story of Your Life, which the film adapts. The story uses Fermat's principle of least time from physics as a key idea, which the film mostly leaves out.
items.why: Rare fiction that takes linguistics and physics seriously. It pairs with this week's topic on the invention of writing.

items.title: Three follow-up questions before your own view
items.topic: active listening and asking better questions
items.description: In one real conversation this week, when someone shares an opinion or a story, ask three follow-up questions before you say what you think. Keep them open: what, how, what was that like.
items.why: Most people jump to their own view. Holding it back for three questions makes the other person feel heard and teaches you more.
steps: Pick one ordinary conversation, at work or with a friend
Ask three open follow-up questions in a row
Only then share your view, and notice whether it changed
items.then: Afterwards, note one thing you learned that you would have missed.

items.title: Turn a room into a camera
items.description: Black out a room's window with card or foil and make a small hole. On a sunny day an upside-down image of the outside appears on the far wall. Painters used this for centuries, and it is the oldest form of a camera.
items.why: Physics you can walk around in. It also changes how you see light in paintings like Hammershøi's.
steps: Pick a room with a window facing a bright view
Cover the window fully and cut a hole about 1 cm wide
Wait a few minutes for your eyes to adjust and look at the wall opposite
Try a smaller hole and see how sharpness and brightness trade off

resources.creator: Getty

cross_domain.connection: The pinhole trade-off between sharpness and brightness is the same one every lens and every painter of light has faced.

items.then: Take a phone photo of the image on the wall and share it with someone.

lessons.title: Saying what you like: 〜が好きです
lessons.explanation: To say you like something, put the thing first, then が好きです (ga suki desu). To ask what someone likes, use 何が好きですか (nani ga suki desu ka). To say you do not really like something, use は instead of が and end with あまり好きじゃないです. It is softer and more polite than a plain no.

examples.romanization: donna eiga ga suki desu ka
examples.meaning: What kind of films do you like?

examples.text: 納豆はあまり好きじゃないです
examples.romanization: nattō wa amari suki ja nai desu

lessons.title: Introducing yourself: నా పేరు
lessons.explanation: To give your name, say నా పేరు (nā pēru, my name) and then your name. To ask someone's name politely, use మీ పేరు ఏమిటి? (mī pēru ēmiṭi?). మీ (mī) is the polite 'your'. End with మిమ్మల్ని కలవడం సంతోషం (mimmalni kalavaḍaṁ santōṣaṁ), nice to meet you.

Practise it with Claude as a short role-play, or with one Telugu speaker you know.
